alt_text: Central plaza at Chavin de Huantar.
caption: Central plaza at Chavin de Huantar. Open plazas, restricted galleries, stairways, and interior passages worked together to stage movement from public gathering into controlled ritual space.
credit: Photo by Martin St-Amant, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

alt_text: Chavin cactus-bearer stele, showing a standing figure holding a cactus staff.
caption: Cactus-bearer stele from Chavin de Huantar. The relief is one of the strongest visual anchors for San Pedro, or huachuma, in Chavin ritual imagery.
credit: Photo by Carlo Brescia / Limaymanta pacha, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

alt_text: The Lanzon at Chavin de Huantar, photographed in the temple gallery.
caption: The Lanzon, a central cult image within the Old Temple gallery. Its restricted placement matters: Chavin ritual power was staged through controlled access, darkness, sound, and encounter.
credit: CyArk, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

alt_text: Black-and-White Portal at Chavin de Huantar.
caption: The Black-and-White Portal, or Portico de las Falconidas. Chavin stonework used thresholds, contrast, and sculptural programs to mark transitions between ritual zones.
credit: Photo by Dtarazona, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

alt_text: Chavin feline-and-cactus stirrup vessel in the Walters Art Museum.
caption: Chavin feline-and-cactus stirrup vessel, 900-200 BCE. Cactus imagery appears in a larger visual grammar of feline, serpent, and transformed bodies.
credit: Walters Art Museum, accession 48.2832, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0; object public domain.
